narratives.line: For a week, governments outside the three powers have made deals without Washington, whose tariffs hit allies as well as rivals.
A US firm's treatment by regulators now depends partly on its closeness to the president, who has money in some of them.
Drones now reach far behind any front, so civilian buildings and roads in countries at peace are being prepared for strikes.
States spy on and sabotage each other through private firms, and governments now leave the firms to defend themselves.
The chipmaker's chief returns with the president's support, and the penalties for chips reaching China fall on firms abroad.
States outside the war now try to move it off their territory, by suing the side that struck or towing a damaged ship away.
Cheaper fuel depends on a pause in the Iran war that Israel is openly lobbying Washington to end.
Governments want payments for health care to pass through channels they control, while they pay doctors and settle claims slowly.
Talks that need every government's consent now fail, while courts that vote and groups that admit only the willing still decide.
The war's attacks now land in countries outside it, and those countries mostly respond by naming the weapon, not by firing back.
AI labs now raise money from the public, and the sums are large enough that other risky assets fall when they do.

narratives.kicker: OLD AGE / INDIVIDUAL ACCOUNTS / THE STATE
narratives.line: In one week, pension saving has been pushed to more workers, so more people's retirement rests on what their own account holds.
The talks after the summit are about lines on land, while both wars are now fought against ships, which no draft yet covers.
For four days running, data people must give the state has been breached as often as data they chose to give shops.
Gold and bitcoin now fall with tech shares, as high rates make every asset bought on borrowed money costly to keep.
Clean power is being built on rivers and reservoirs already promised to farms and homes, so choosing energy now means rationing water.
As private money pulls back from data centres, states now offer to decide where they are built and to carry their losses.
Through a fortnight of school and campus protests, states have met the young with police and courts, and now with call-up plans.
A peace declared by three powers has led the countries near them to build bases and close borders, not to stand down.
Allies left out of the three-power meeting now seek their own talks with Moscow rather than wait for Washington to speak for them.
Ordinary savers could buy an AI lab only after its first-day doubling, while the shares they already held fell that day.

narratives.kicker: ORGANISED CRIME / MILITARY FORCE / DUE PROCESS
narratives.line: Gangs and smugglers are now fought by armies and foreign troops, so suspects are killed as enemies rather than charged in court.
Outside Europe, strikes this fortnight have mostly been to collect pay already owed or promised, often by a state short of money.
The AI boom is now being sold to the public before it makes a profit, while those already rich from it buy older assets.
Countries relying on missile defence are protected only as long as stocks last, and refilling them takes years.
While three powers bargain over two wars, other governments sign trade deals among themselves rather than wait on the result.
Flaws found by AI now arrive faster than fixes can be tested, so the repairs themselves are taking systems down.
The chip scandal has not cut the chipmaker's sales, and the burden of proof now falls on the countries its chips pass through.
Before leaders meet over two wars, each side strikes bridges and islands, the crossings a settlement would have to assign.

narratives.kicker: COST OF LIVING / THE STREET / COMPENSATION
narratives.line: Two weeks of protest over prices and rents have been met with wage and pension top-ups, while the energy shock behind prices goes on.
Outages from updates, flaws and attacks now come in the same week, and users cannot tell which kind has hit them.
After this week's Microsoft and air traffic failures, the fallback for shared digital systems is left to households and staff.
Five years after Russia's 2021 draft treaties, NATO's shape is bargained in talks Europe does not lead.
Five years into the price rise, incomes set by formula or grant have fallen furthest behind, and their holders now protest or close.
Five years of high food prices and cut supply routes have put governments back into selling food and choosing which crops are grown.
With Nvidia's chief gone, the scandal is a dispute over which US department and which Asian hub let chips reach China.
Public services from air traffic to police email now run on single systems, and stop entirely when one of them fails.
Talks to end the wars with Russia and Iran now run alongside strikes on bases, ships and oil sites far from any front.
Four years into the AI boom, one firm's chief or one firm's servers can move markets and stop office work on several continents.
Leaders' children who took office or business roles on a parent's name now face resignations, trials and conflict-of-interest rows.
With crude below $90, governments still set what drivers and ferry passengers pay for fuel and cover the gap from budgets.
With two wars unsettled, entry to a country, a competition or peace talks is granted or refused as a bargaining move in them.
With oil output back near pre-war levels, producers and buyers now invest as if the Strait of Hormuz will stay unsafe.
Housing is now fought over at work, where unions strike over rents and employers and payroll funds are asked to supply homes.
Eighteen months in, the first pope from the Americas takes sides in South American politics and holds back German reform.
Membership of alliances and talks is now a tool of pressure, withdrawn from members who turn away and offered to others on conditions.
While Washington and Tehran negotiate, attacks linked to Iran are moving to European shops and to US air bases in Britain.
Nearly five years into the invasion, talks to end it advance while EU governments argue over which of them pays for Ukraine.
Four years after ChatGPT, the chipmakers that supply the AI labs are buying stakes in them as the labs turn to the stock market.
Espionage against states and firms now goes through the private lives and phone numbers of the people who hold their secrets.
Four years after ChatGPT, so much rests on one chip firm that its chief's private life moves share prices and chip policy.
Oil prices now follow what Trump says about Iran talks more than the attacks on the Saudi pipeline that bypasses Hormuz.
As the last four years are confirmed the hottest, governments seek new gas and LNG while the climate summit plans electrification.
With the US-Iran war paused, Washington presses Iran by land and sea while Saudi Arabia and the Houthis trade strikes.
Courts now reach presidents and their deputies through their assets and declared wealth, while elsewhere they try the opposition.
Legal routes to work abroad are now so few that they go by lottery, while irregular routes still kill dozens at a time.
Twenty-five years after joining the WTO, Chinese makers sell abroad at luxury prices as well as low ones.
With the Iran war unresolved, governments are ending the fuel tax cuts that kept the war's price off drivers.
A year after Washington ended its EV credit, US makers drop electric pickups while Chinese makers price higher and sell abroad.
Governments are using pardons and refusals to sign laws, and courts and heads of state are now being asked to overrule them.
El Niño is expected to bring drought, but its first weeks have brought storms and landslides to mountain cities and the Pacific coast.
The war's energy shock is now an order book for turbines, batteries and solar cells, and the factories making them are at capacity.
Regulators now treat the recommendation system, not the single post, as the thing a platform must answer for.
A failed bank or state fund turns into a case against the presidents and judges near it, and its fines divide governments for years.
Homes in growing cities are now priced by money earned elsewhere, so a rise in local wages no longer buys a place to live.
Democrats' talk of a data-centre moratorium has cut share prices across Asia, where growth now rests on building AI.
The war's oil price now pushes rates up in countries that buy oil, while central banks in countries that sell it cut.
Parliaments are refusing governments' budgets, so next year's tax and spending are set in the chamber rather than the cabinet.
Governments now send soldiers to keep ordinary civil order at home, and police seek rules on force closer to a soldier's.
The Iran war's price rise has now cost Trump's party Congress, and central banks abroad still hold rates high against it.
The bodies that run the count and draw the maps are now fought over before the vote, though the US redrawing failed on Tuesday.
Abroad the midterm rout is read as a verdict on each capital's dispute with Washington, while the president still runs the war.
Four years after ChatGPT, responsibility for AI's errors is being placed on those who adopt it rather than on those who build it.

narratives.kicker: A STRAIT / WHO PAYS / WHO GAINS
narratives.line: With Hormuz shut, the war's cost falls on energy importers and its gains go to producers whose oil does not pass the strait.
Large breaches now start with a firm's suppliers or its staff rather than its own systems, and the firm still bears the loss.
Cheap, unclaimed threats against Poland's flights, satellite links and border now draw costly military and police responses.
Eight years into the US-China tariff war, producers elsewhere merge to compete with Chinese goods or tax them at the border.
Four years after ChatGPT, AI firms fund their build with borrowed money, while governments and voters set terms for its data centres.
Hacking now reaches shop freezers and exchange wallets, and the EU calls an attack on refrigeration an attack on food supply.
Parties in office now shape who votes and which ballots count before polling day, not only dispute results after it.
Markets now price a negotiated end to the war with Iran faster than the fighting around the Strait of Hormuz is slowing.
With the US midterms due on 3 November, the choice between striking Iran and talking to it is being timed to an American vote.
Five years after the storming of the Capitol, parties in office are now as likely as their opponents to cast doubt on a count.
As everyday payment moves to phones and cards, its cost reaches the payer as interest or data rather than as a visible fee.
Six years after pandemic aid, budgets protect pensions and salaried staff while the self-employed and claimants are left with less.
Four years after ChatGPT, AI spending is so concentrated that one chip firm's staff gain years of pay as another's shares fall 29%.
As talks to end the war with Iran stall, governments are judged on its fuel price and at least one now takes more of it in tax.
A decade after Poland's court dispute began, constitutions and courts are where governments and their opponents fight.
More than a year after Nepal's Gen Z protests, Europe's governments meet their own young protesters mainly with police numbers.
Taiwan's fastest growth in fifty years rests on AI spending, so when US tech shares fall its state funds and central bank step in.
With oil near $118, the war's price rise is now argued over in wage talks, while governments cut fuel and sales taxes to slow it.
More than four years into the invasion, European ministers shun Russia while Washington and African governments negotiate with it.
Protests called for the same weekend in several European countries are met with bans in some cities and negotiation in others.
AI investment now drives a large part of US growth, while investors mark down the companies doing the spending.
Before the US midterms, Washington is pressing for a lower oil price in two wars, and fuel taxes and budgets elsewhere are reset.
Since the Capitol riot of 2021, governing parties and losing candidates alike treat the vote count as something to contest.
Cheap drones have made defence a matter of quantity again, so states are financing arms factories and widening conscription.
The Iran war's price rise holds central bank rates up, and households meet it as the highest mortgage rates in over a decade.
The AI data centre lifts profits at Asian hardware makers and has become a planning and security dispute in Europe.
Former heads of government face courts at home, and their allies answer with amnesty bills, new laws and foreign refuge.
Backup systems meant to catch human error failed on railways and grids this week, and official blame still starts with the operator.
The Iran war's fuel squeeze reaches US air fares, easyJet luggage, Estonian asphalt and Malaysian subsidies
The US figures in Flávio Bolsonaro's exit, Lula's sovereignty warning, Colombian drills and Machado's return
Patients in Canada, adult children in Germany and pharmacy users in India pay where public schemes fall short
Nigeria's electoral body, New Zealand employers and an Australian court handle AI-made faces and files
China dropped La Liga, an Indian court an Adani film, and a Korean drama faces calls to stop over Gwangju
Trump called Brazil's election rigged while offering $1 million for evidence of fraud in US elections
Anthropic filed for a record US share listing as Elvis Presley's rights holders sued it over 200 songs
The Hormuz oil shock is raising US petrol and European gas prices while Iran hosts Gulf security talks
Students are on strike or occupying buildings in France, Mexico, India and Italy, with Serbia next
Egypt, Indonesia and Tamil Nadu are expanding housing while Portugal investigates police at housing protests
Money is slipping into dollars, gold and trusts, and the state is answering with discounts.
AI is paying the clerk to leave, and the ditch, the field and the rubble still take the labourer.
Before the dead come back, every rite is being measured: hosts, incense sticks, costumes and knees.
The cloud has come down to the county, and the county has started saying no.
Europe is asking households to last 72 hours alone while its states shop for other people's warheads.
A ballot cast in Brazil is being counted in Buenos Aires, Madrid and Nairobi.
A company has written down the end of the world as a risk factor, and the market has bought it.
The Gulf is running two clocks: one for the talks, one for the strike.
One machine is cutting the power, guarding the lake, carrying the wounded, and selling itself.
For one night the whole world agreed about a football.
Courts are re-sentencing 1979 and 1996, and a library is removing 2026.
Students have toppled a government, and a president is doing a teenage dance.
